units.t: Close Reading and Citing Strong Evidence

learn: Close reading means reading a passage several times, each time looking deeper.
Annotate as you read: underline key details, circle unfamiliar words, write questions and reactions in the margin.
Annotations become the raw material for analysis and essays.
lessons.try: Annotate a page of a short story with at least ten notes.

learn: Eighth graders cite the evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly and what it implies.
Thorough evidence covers the claim fully; strong evidence leaves little room for doubt.
Weigh several quotes and choose the one that does the most work.
check: Analysis covers what the text says explicitly and what it...
lessons.try: For one claim, collect four quotes and justify which is strongest.

learn: Evidence alone never proves a point; your commentary must explain how it does.
A useful ratio is two sentences of explanation for every quotation.
Explain word choice, implications and connections to the claim.
check: A useful ratio is ___ sentences of commentary per quote.
lessons.try: Write a paragraph with one quote and two sentences of commentary.

learn: Determine a theme and analyse its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to characters, setting and plot.
Themes often emerge through conflict and change.
Charles Dickens's "A Christmas Carol" (1843) develops the theme that people can change through compassion.
lessons.try: Trace how Scrooge's change develops the theme across the five staves.

learn: Universal themes appear across cultures and centuries: courage, loss, identity, justice.
Ancient myths and modern novels may share a theme.
Compare how different texts handle the same universal theme.
check: Different texts may handle the same theme...
lessons.try: Compare a myth and a modern story that share a theme.

learn: An objective summary of a literary text includes theme, key events and how they relate, without personal opinion.
Keep it brief: usually under a fifth of the original's length.
Use present tense and your own words.
check: A summary is much ___ than the original.
lessons.try: Write a summary of "A Christmas Carol" in 150 words.

learn: Analyse how particular lines of dialogue or incidents propel the action, reveal character or provoke a decision.
A single line can change a story's direction.
Look for turning points in conversations.
check: A single line can provoke a...
lessons.try: Find a line of dialogue that changes the direction of a story.

learn: Authors choose how to structure a text: flashbacks, parallel plots, foreshadowing, cliffhangers.
Structure creates effects like mystery, tension or surprise.
Edgar Allan Poe's "The Tell-Tale Heart" (1843) uses a nervous first-person narrator to build suspense.
check: A cliffhanger ends a section with...
lessons.try: Analyse how Poe structures "The Tell-Tale Heart" to build tension.

learn: Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows something the characters don't.
This difference creates suspense or humour.
Authors control what readers know and when.
check: Dramatic irony is when the audience knows...
lessons.try: Explain how dramatic irony works in a story or play you know.

units.t: Word Choice, Tone and Figurative Language

learn: Word choice shapes meaning and tone.
Connotations carry feelings: "home" feels warmer than "house".
Analyse the impact of specific words on tone.
lessons.try: Rewrite a paragraph changing five words to shift its tone.

learn: An analogy compares two things to explain an idea.
An allusion refers to a well-known person, place, story or event: "He met his Waterloo."
Allusions often come from mythology, the Bible, Shakespeare and history.
lessons.try: Find three allusions in everyday speech and explain them.

learn: Verbal irony: saying the opposite of what you mean.
Situational irony: the opposite of what is expected happens.
Puns play on words with more than one meaning.
check: Saying "Great weather!" in a storm is...
A fire station burning down is...
Words with more than one meaning
lessons.try: Write an example of verbal irony, situational irony and a pun.

learn: Lyric poems express personal feelings. Narrative poems tell stories. Dramatic monologues are spoken by a character.
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's "Paul Revere's Ride" (1860) is a narrative poem.
Form helps convey meaning.
check: A poem that tells a story is...
lessons.try: Read "Paul Revere's Ride" and identify its story elements.

learn: Rhythm, rhyme and repetition create music in poetry.
Enjambment runs a sentence across a line break; end-stopped lines pause at the end.
A refrain is a repeated line or phrase.
check: A sentence running past a line break is...
lessons.try: Mark enjambment and end-stopped lines in a poem.

learn: Read a poem aloud, then ask: who is speaking, to whom, and why?
Consider imagery, figurative language and shifts in tone.
Paul Laurence Dunbar's "We Wear the Mask" (1895) explores hiding pain behind smiles.
check: A shift in tone is a change in...
lessons.try: Write an interpretation of "We Wear the Mask".

units.t: Drama and Comparing Texts Across Forms

learn: Plays are read differently from novels: attend to stage directions, dialogue and what's left unsaid.
Imagine the staging: set, lighting, movement.
Subtext is the meaning beneath the words.
lessons.try: Read a scene and describe how you'd stage it.

learn: Shakespeare's comedies end in marriages; tragedies end in deaths.
His language includes iambic pentameter and invented words still used today.
"A Midsummer Night's Dream" mixes lovers, workers and fairies.
lessons.try: Read a scene from "A Midsummer Night's Dream" aloud with classmates.

learn: Analyse how a film or live production stays faithful to or departs from the text.
Evaluate directors' and actors' choices.
Different forms reveal different strengths.
check: A production may ___ from the text.
lessons.try: Compare a scene in a play with a recorded performance.

learn: Analyse how specific sentences and paragraphs develop and refine key concepts.
Note how authors use headings, transitions and examples.
Paragraph structure supports the overall argument.
lessons.try: Explain the role of each paragraph in an essay.

lessons.t: Point of View and Conflicting Evidence
learn: Determine an author's point of view and how they respond to conflicting evidence or viewpoints.
Strong writers acknowledge opposing views fairly.
Compare two texts that disagree on facts or interpretation.
check: Point of view is an author's...
lessons.try: Read two articles on the same issue and identify where they disagree.

learn: Delineate and evaluate an argument: is the reasoning sound and the evidence relevant and sufficient?
Recognise when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
Frederick Douglass's 1852 speech "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?" is a powerful argument.
lessons.try: Evaluate the reasoning in a famous historical speech.

learn: Write a precise claim and distinguish it from alternate or opposing claims.
A precise claim is specific and arguable.
"School should start at 9 a.m. to improve teen sleep" is precise.
check: School should start at 9 a.m. to improve sleep
A claim must be distinguished from...
lessons.try: Make three vague claims precise.

learn: Support claims with logical reasoning and credible evidence.
Use a mix: statistics, expert quotes, examples.
Explain the warrant: why the evidence supports the claim.
check: A mix of evidence makes arguments...
lessons.try: Write a body paragraph with a statistic, an expert quote and your explanation.

learn: Address counterarguments fairly and respond with rebuttals.
Use transitions that clarify relationships among claims, reasons and evidence.
Conclude by reinforcing the claim and its significance.
lessons.try: Write a full argumentative essay of five paragraphs.

learn: Verbals are verb forms used as other parts of speech.
Gerunds act as nouns ("Swimming is fun"). Participles act as adjectives ("the broken window"). Infinitives use "to" ("I want to win").
Verbals add variety to sentences.
lessons.try: Write a sentence with each type of verbal.

learn: Active voice: the subject acts ("The team won the game").
Passive voice: the subject receives the action ("The game was won by the team").
Use active voice for clarity; passive when the doer is unknown or unimportant.
check: Passive works when the doer is...
lessons.try: Change five passive sentences to active.

learn: Indicative mood states facts ("She runs"). Imperative gives commands ("Run!").
Interrogative asks questions. Conditional shows possibility ("I would run").
Subjunctive expresses wishes or contrary-to-fact ideas ("If I were you...").
lessons.try: Write sentences in all five moods.

learn: Conduct short research projects that answer a question, drawing on several sources.
Generate additional focused questions for further research.
Quote and paraphrase while avoiding plagiarism; follow a standard citation format.
lessons.try: Research a historical event and write a two-page report with citations.

learn: Engage readers with a strong opening, a clear point of view and a well-paced sequence.
Use dialogue, pacing, description and reflection.
Use transitions to signal shifts in time or setting.
lessons.try: Write a short story with a flashback.

learn: Present claims and findings with relevant evidence, sound reasoning and well-chosen details.
Use eye contact, adequate volume and clear pronunciation.
Integrate multimedia to clarify information.
lessons.try: Give a three-minute presentation with a visual aid.
